text: hey everybody every time I make a video where I point out that the Bible has no inherent meaning I always get a lot of push back from folks who either don't
understand precisely what I'm saying or think I'm just profoundly mistaken so I want to use a couple of illustrations to show you what I mean by that but first I
want to describe the process of making meaning with a text from the perspective of cognitive Linguistics when we read a
text there are two phases of comprehension that go on in our minds and they happen subconsciously and very
very rapidly almost instantaneously so it can feel like meaning is just popping into our brains but what's going on is
our minds are looking at a given linguistic expression and then generating all the possible meanings
that could be intended by that linguistic expression and then using the context nonlinguistic cues and
everything around us our minds try to whittle down those potential meanings to what we believe was most likely intended
and this process is overwhelmingly good enough we can successfully communicate most of the
time because this process has become very refined and very accurate but it's not perfect and here's one example of
this uh if we go into the Bible the new testament's book of Jude there's only one chapter and in verse 22 it says but of some have compassion making a
difference now for years I've asked people what precise prely they think this verse is trying to say and every
single person I've ever asked has interpreted it along the lines of when we have compassion on people we can have a positive influence or a positive
impact on their lives and that's a wonderful message and it makes sense of the text but it has absolutely nothing
to do with what was intended by the King James translators and here's why when we look at that and our minds generate all
the potential meanings the meaning that it is able to generate are based on our experiences with and understandings of
the agreements that have been arrived at by people regarding what kind of semantic content is going to be linked
with what kinds of sounds words phrases Clauses and then we Whittle down from there if you have never had experience
with or if you don't have understanding of a specific relationship that someone might intend you're not going to be able
to generate that potential meaning at the same time if you are able to generate uh the correct meaning among
the potential meanings but then for whatever reason Whittle it down to the wrong meaning you're also going to miss the mark but the important thing to keep
in mind here is that the meaning is always entirely in our minds our minds are generating the meaning the meaning never leaves our minds so what does
jude2 mean well the notion of making a difference being connected with this concept of having a positive impact or a
positive influence was not something that people agreed on until around the year 1900 but the King James version was
translated in 1611 and they had a different agreement back then regarding the semantic content that would be
associated with that phrase back then making a difference meant making a distinction exercising discernment
distinguishing between things and so the King James translators were trying to say of some have compassion but be
Discerning now here's another example of how this idea of uh experience with and understanding of those relationships can
help or hinder our understanding when I was a kid and our family would go out to eat at a restaurant which was a rare occurrence but when it did happen
servers would ask us what we wanted to drink and I would say a Coke and then they would respond what kind and then I
would say a Sprite or a root beer or something like that now if that sounds unusual to you it's probably because you
don't have a bunch of experience with or understanding of this use of the word Coke as a generic reference to any soda

our servers in those instances would be aware of that agreement and so they would know to ask what kind rather than

to be linked with what sounds and words and phrases and clauses and when we're talking about ancient texts from thousands of years ago there's no
metaphysical mean meaning somehow inhabiting these texts that we get a little chisel and a hammer to excavate uh that's just not how meaning works we
have to generate all the potential meaning in our minds and then try to use the available Clues to whittle it down to what we think was most likely
intended so going back to Jude the King James translators were using a pretty late manuscript and the word that we
translate making a difference was in the nominative case meaning it is associated with the subject of the verb
we now know that it was intended to be in the accusative case we have much earlier and more reliable manuscripts that have that word in the accusative
case meaning this is not um associated with the people who are doing The Compassion having it is associated with
the objects of the compassion in other words we're supposed to be having compassion on these people who are
making a distinction so the original author of The epistle of Jude was trying to say have compassion on some of those
who are making a distinction so what does that mean well there are a lot of potential meanings this could mean
someone who is wavering this could mean someone who is criticizing this could mean someone who is inside or outside
the group this could mean a lot of different things and so we have to try to generate the potential meanings that could have been intended here and then
somehow Whittle them down to what was most like the intended and that process involves trying to understand the
circumstances as best we can trying to understand the linguistic conventions and patterns from that time period as best we can trying to understand the
contextual Clues as best we can to try to arrive at what we think is most likely and unfortunately that's not an
exact science that is something that is frequently going to be influenced by what we want the text to mean what we
may have said in the past and we want to defend our earlier conclusions we don't want to be wrong we don't want to change
what we're thinking um it can be influenced by a lot of different things but the more critical and the more informed the scholarship more carefully
we're going to try to reconstruct what may have been intended by the original authors rather than what might make the
text more meaningful or useful to us and this is one of the issues with apologetics uh apologists will try to
create all those potential meanings then they will Whittle things down based on what is most useful and helpful for them
rather than what was most likely intended by the original authors and editors in their original sets of
circumstances for their original audiences and so when we're making meaning with texts we have different
options that we can choose from and the question is what are we doing to whittle them down are we just relying on our own
intuition which is going to be guided by what we want and what is going to make us feel better or are we overruling those to try to more consciously and
intentionally reconstruct the meaning that might have been most meaningful and most useful to that ancient author thousands of years ago who might have
very different concerns from our own so when I say the Bible has no inherent meaning that's what I mean all of the
meaning is generated by us and then whittel down to what we think is most likely and if we're not careful if we're
not consciously trying to whittle things down based on Ancient context rather than modern ones we are just going to be
reading what we want into the text rather than trying to understand the text on the terms of the original
